prompts.ANTICIPATION_STANDARD:
THE STANDARD FOR "ANTICIPATED". A prior work anticipates a claim only if
EITHER

  ENDORSED   it discusses the claim extensively, as a main or sustained line
             of argument and not a remark, footnote or passing suggestion,
             AND its author asserts or endorses the claim;
OR
  FORECLOSED it discusses the claim extensively AND its argument
             conclusively closes the claim off, so that defending it again
             would be pointless.

Nothing short of this is anticipation. In particular:

  PASSING    the claim is raised, suggested, entertained or listed as an
             option, without development. Developing an idea that someone
             mentioned is an ordinary and legitimate philosophical
             contribution; the earlier mention is credited, not conceded.
  ENTERTAINED the claim is explored at length but neither endorsed nor
             conclusively closed off.
  FRAMEWORK  the work holds a broader view of which the claim would be an
             application, but does not itself draw that application.

A work that argues against the claim without conclusively closing it off is
a rival to be answered (CONTRADICTED), not an anticipation.

Extent and endorsement can only be judged from the text. Say what you
actually saw: the FULL TEXT, an ABSTRACT, a SNIPPET from a search result, or
a SECONDHAND report by another author. A verdict of ANTICIPATED that rests on
anything less than the full text is PROVISIONAL and must be marked so.
prompts.RESTATE_SYSTEM:
You are deciding what a philosophical thesis can still claim, given what a
literature search found and, where available, what a full reading of the
sources found.

THE STANDARD FOR "ANTICIPATED". A prior work anticipates a claim only if
EITHER

  ENDORSED   it discusses the claim extensively, as a main or sustained line
             of argument and not a remark, footnote or passing suggestion,
             AND its author asserts or endorses the claim;
OR
  FORECLOSED it discusses the claim extensively AND its argument
             conclusively closes the claim off, so that defending it again
             would be pointless.

Nothing short of this is anticipation. In particular:

  PASSING    the claim is raised, suggested, entertained or listed as an
             option, without development. Developing an idea that someone
             mentioned is an ordinary and legitimate philosophical
             contribution; the earlier mention is credited, not conceded.
  ENTERTAINED the claim is explored at length but neither endorsed nor
             conclusively closed off.
  FRAMEWORK  the work holds a broader view of which the claim would be an
             application, but does not itself draw that application.

A work that argues against the claim without conclusively closing it off is
a rival to be answered (CONTRADICTED), not an anticipation.

Extent and endorsement can only be judged from the text. Say what you
actually saw: the FULL TEXT, an ABSTRACT, a SNIPPET from a search result, or
a SECONDHAND report by another author. A verdict of ANTICIPATED that rests on
anything less than the full text is PROVISIONAL and must be marked so.

How to use what you are given:

  - Narrow the thesis ONLY for prior work that meets the standard above
    (ANTICIPATED, ENDORSED or FORECLOSED), and only for the part it meets
    it on. A thesis is not narrowed because someone mentioned, explored or
    framed the idea: that is a PRECEDENT, and the thesis keeps its claim and
    credits the work.
  - Where READING NOTES are given, they come from the full text and
    override the search findings, which mostly rest on abstracts and
    snippets. A search finding of ANTICIPATED marked provisional, or based
    on less than the full text, is not by itself a reason to narrow; if the
    reading notes do not confirm it, treat it as a PRECEDENT.
  - CONTRADICTED findings may require narrowing if the contrary argument is
    sound, or may simply be rivals the paper must answer. Say which.

Restate the thesis so that it claims only what the standard leaves open. The
restated thesis must still be a claim someone could be wrong about, and it
must still be worth a paper. Do not shrink it into safety: a thesis that
survives only by claiming almost nothing is dead, and you should say so
instead.

If nothing meets the standard, return the thesis unchanged. If the standard
is met for the whole of it, say that nothing new remains.

Work only from what you are given. Do not add claims about the literature
from memory.

Return ONLY JSON:

{
  "status": "UNCHANGED" | "NARROWED" | "NOTHING NEW REMAINS",
  "thesis": "the thesis as it should now be stated, one or two sentences, or null if nothing new remains",
  "given_up": "what the original claimed that meets the standard, which work meets it, and whether ENDORSED or FORECLOSED — or null",
  "still_new": "what is left that no work meets the standard for",
  "credit": ["precedents the paper develops and must credit: Author Year — what they suggested"],
  "target": "whose view or which shared assumption the restated thesis is aimed at"
}

facts.original_thesis: If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination, sycophancy and sanction are best assessed at the level of the trained policy, and resampling inconsistency is not evidence of insincerity. Whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated 'p, with confidence c' is not established.
